body:
I don't think we really discussed this much actually. @dglazkov, @smaug----, @hayatoito, @rniwa? Now would be a good time to decide on this, since I'm working on several patches to HTML that would be affected by this.

"In a light document" (to disambiguate) and "connected" (after the developer-facing API)?

"light document" sounds a bit odd, given all the different meanings of "light". One could think data documents being "light", since they are less heavy than documents bound to a browsing context.
And there is no shadow document. 

To me in a document clearly means light dom only, since there is parentNode chain from node to document in that case. That is what tree structures usually mean in computer science.
But I guess I could live with "in a document's light DOM".

I'd say "directly in a document" or "in a document without crossing shadow boundary" or "in a document tree".

I'm opposed to using either "light DOM" or "light document" since "light" would be yet another arbitrary jargon we need to remember.

The DOM Standard does already introduce "light tree" as an opposite to "shadow tree", but given this feedback I'm inclined to just stick with "in a document" and "in a shadow-including document" meaning what they mean today.

> To me in a document clearly means light dom only, since there is parentNode chain from node to document in that case. That is what tree structures usually mean in computer science.

Is that CS tree concept usually denoted using the word "in", or is there perhaps a more precise phrase?

I do think "in a document tree" (and "in a shadow-including document tree" or similar) helps a bit over the simple "in a document". It makes me aware that there's a concept known as "document tree" and that I should be thinking in terms of tree structures.

I like "in a light document"/"in a document's light DOM" and "connected" the most but I guess others don't.

"in a light document" doesn't quite make sense, but the the others are fine.

(Though, very subjective view, I prefer Gecko's naming: In composed document, in uncomposed document, but I think others have said they don't like those.)

> I'm inclined to just stick with "in a document" and "in a shadow-including document" meaning what they mean today.

+1

I am also fine with "in a document tree", for "in a document". That might be helpful because we can track our progress easily. If we we encounter an "in a document" in the spec, that means we have to replace it with either "in a document tree" or "in a shadow-including document". If we encounter an "in a document tree", that means the replacement was already done.

We should not use "light". "light" does not have an absolute meaning. Its meaning is just a parent tree of a shadow tree, in my feeling... Whether "light tree" is a document tree or a shadow tree depends on its context.
I defer to y'all. No strong opinions, except that it should be great and amazing.

Since we should probably make a decision on this before spreading the terminology to too many specs. I see two potential issues being discussed here:
- "in a document" confuses some people (see my OP)
- "in a shadow-including document" could simply be "connected" or "connected to a document" for consistency with the callback naming

I'm OK keeping things as-is. But I think changing "in a document" to either "in a document tree" or "directly in a document" would be a nice improvement. And similarly I think using "connected" consistently would be kind of nice.

I don't think anyone feels very strongly here though (besides some people not liking certain proposed alternative terms) so maybe we should just keep things as they are?
Indeed, changing "in a document" to "in a document tree" would be a good improvement.

We started using "connected" in HTML for being inserted into a shadow-including document. That matches the callbacks more closely. In a shadow-including document is state, which we don't really expose through callbacks.

"In a document tree" seems fine, though will result in a bit of churn. Probably manageable.

Yeah, I did not have a strong opinion, but I am feeling that we could get benefits if we could have shorter, intuitive, terminologies.

Basically, I like using _connected_ as a replacement of _shadow-including_. Thus, the proposal from me is:

To represet state:
- _is connected to a document_   (As a replacement of _in a shadow-including document_)
- A and B _are connected to the same document_  (As a replacement of _in the same shadow-including document_ in https://github.com/whatwg/dom/pull/273)

To represent a change of state:
- _get connected to a document_ (As a replacement of  _is connected_)
- _get disconnected from a document_ (As a replacement of _is disconnected_)

Is using _is_ and _get_ in this way confusing? I am not 100% sure whether this is a good idea or not.
As far as I know,  _connectedCallback_, _disconnectedCallback_ and _Node.isConnected_ are only Web-exposed names around here.

I also like using 'in a document tree' to avoid confusion of 'in a document'.
- _in a document tree_ (as a replacement of _in a document_)
- _in a shadow tree_
@domenic @rniwa, thoughts? I would be okay with "is connected", "got connected", and "got disconnected" (I don't think we need to add "document" as the APIs don't have it either).

"becomes" instead of "got" IMO, but that sounds nice otherwise.

Do you have a proposal for a replacement for "in the same shadow-including document," which pointer lock wants? (IMO in that case it's fine to just talk about having the same shadow-including root.)

Are you on board with "in a document tree" as well? As was pointed out previously, this gives us a nice division: "in a document" means "not yet updated for shadow DOM" whereas "in a document tree" or "connected" imply we've spent the time and figured out what should happen.

I'm okay with renaming "in a document", yes. "Becomes" also seems okay.

And yeah, for "same" we should figure out if that can't just talk about the shadow-including root instead. Seems like a better abstraction.
Yeah, I was gonna suggest "becomes connected" and "becomes disconnected" as well.

Thanks. It looks the conclusion is:

We will use:
- "is connected"
- "becomes connected" / "becomes disconnected"
- "in a document tree" / "in a shadow tree"

Maybe we might want to have the following too:
- "A and B are connected to the same document"

I am okay with these.
How often do we need "A and B are connected to the same document"? That's basically "A and B are connected and their node document is identical".

I can not tell how often we need it.

Until we start to feel we need it, let's use "A and B are connected and their node document (shadow-including root?) is identical". That should be enough.
I guess both node document and shadow-including root work there due to the way connected is defined.
Ah, I did not realize that [node document](https://dom.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-node-document) is clearly defined. Thanks!

I created #275 and https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/1483 to fix this, however I'm not sure I'm entirely happy with the result. There's a couple cases in HTML where "in a document" is used and then there's also reference made to that document's browsing context. It's not clear if that works well with "in a document tree".

And "is connected" often gets awkward since a lot of checks are for the opposite scenario. So just using "connected" is a term there might be better.

"Becomes connected" and "becomes disconnected" seem to work fine, although how build on top of insertion and removal is a little wonky, but we're not changing that here.

I think "connected" instead of "is connected" makes sense.

I think we should leave "in a document", giving it a definition like:

**In a document** means one of either connected or in a document tree. It is a legacy term indicating that the author of the spec that uses it has not yet thought through the interaction of their spec with shadow DOM and made a decision between those two. All uses of it should be replaced with one of the two more precise alternatives as soon as possible.

The meaning of in a document should not change. If a spec hasn't been updated to deal with shadow DOM, features relying on in-a-document should not work. Otherwise the behavior can be somewhat random or reveal parts of the shadow dom accidentally to light DOM etc.

Or did I misunderstand "In a document means one of either connected or in a document tree". Is that missing a question mark, or did you propose in-a-document would just mean 'connected' ?

Hmm, OK. Maybe then

**In a document** means in a document tree. It is a legacy term indicating that the author of the spec that uses it has not yet thought through the interaction of their spec with shadow DOM and made a decision between in a document tree and connected. For now we assume that in a document tree is the correct interpretation, but all uses of in a document should over time be replaced by either in a document tree or connected as appropriate to the specific case in question.

Or maybe this idea of using "in a document" to track not-yet-updatedness is not good?

It sounds fine to have something like that. It's a signal folks can use, but it's not one you can rely on. (Even without "in a document" usage some specification might not have considered shadow trees.)
I updated both PRs.
